candidate.answerReason: Subtracting the equations gives (1−m)x=1. This is impossible when m=1 and supplies a real solution when m≠1.

methods.label: Eliminate y
methods.explanation:
Both equations have the same left side, so subtracting them eliminates \(y\). Any common solution must satisfy
\[
0=(1-m)x-1,
\]
or \((1-m)x=1\).

If \(m=1\), this would say \(0=1\), so there is no solution.

If \(m\ne1\), choose
\[
x=\frac{1}{1-m},\qquad y=mx+3.
\]
These are real numbers. The two original right sides differ by \((1-m)x-1=0\), so this pair satisfies both equations.

Therefore the equations have at least one real solution exactly when \(\boxed{m\ne1}\), choice D.
methods.levelReason: Elementary subtraction reduces the system to one linear equation. Separating the zero-coefficient case avoids division by zero and proves both necessity and existence.
